lessons.dimension: L2 LO2 bottle ageing: red colour
lessons.assertion: A youthful red may show purple or ruby colours; development can introduce garnet or tawny shades, particularly at the rim, and very old or oxidised wine may appear brown. Colour also depends on the grape, production and storage, so it cannot establish an exact age or prove improved quality.

citations.locator: Printed page 11, Colour: red development and oxidation; general observations only

lessons.dimension: L2 LO2 bottle ageing: white colour
lessons.assertion: A pale lemon-coloured white can become deeper gold as it develops; very old or oxidised examples may acquire amber or brown tones. Initial colour, production and storage also matter, so a deeper colour alone proves neither a precise bottle age nor beneficial development.

citations.locator: Printed page 11, Colour: white development and oxidation; no tasting grid or assessment wording reproduced

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 grape-growing label: vintage
lessons.assertion: The vintage identifies the year the grapes were harvested, rather than the year the wine was bottled or released. Local rules determine what proportion must come from that harvest. The year alone does not establish quality; weather, place, grapes and production must be considered together.

citations.locator: Vintage heading: harvest year and the role of weather
PDF page 34, Vintage Date: harvest year and different named-appellation proportions; no US percentage asserted worldwide

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 vine-age label: old vine / Vieilles vignes
lessons.assertion: Vieilles vignes means old vines. Vine age can be relevant to yield and fruit character, but the wording alone guarantees neither concentration nor quality. Definitions, certification and enforceable labelling conditions differ by jurisdiction or scheme; check the producer and applicable rules rather than assume one worldwide legal threshold.

citations.locator: Other terms: old vines / Vieilles vignes
OIV-VITI 703-2024: definitions and recommendations, not a universal national labelling law

lessons.dimension: Vine-age labels: definition versus enforceable law
lessons.assertion: The OIV adopted a definition of an individual old vine with officially documented age of at least 35 years; for a grafted plant, the scion–rootstock union must also have remained intact for at least 35 years. This international recommendation does not automatically impose the same labelling law in every country.

citations.locator: OIV-VITI 703-2024: old-vine definition and harmonisation recommendation

lessons.dimension: L3 vine-age context: individual vine versus parcel
lessons.assertion: In the OIV 2024 definition, an old vineyard is a homogeneous, continuous and legally delimited vineyard parcel with at least 85% of its vines meeting the individual old-vine definition, producing vitivinicultural products eligible for lawful certification by a competent authority. A qualifying vine and a qualifying whole parcel are distinct; this recommendation is not an automatic worldwide labelling permission.

citations.locator: OIV-VITI 703-2024: old-vineyard definition

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 grape-growing label: late harvest / Vendanges tardives
lessons.assertion: Late harvest indicates grapes left on the vine for a later harvest, usually seeking greater ripeness or concentration; Vendanges Tardives is the French wording. The term does not universally require noble rot or guarantee the same finished sweetness. Named origins apply their own conditions, and fermentation determines how much sugar remains.

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 geographical indication: meaning
lessons.assertion: A wine geographical indication identifies an origin associated with the grapes and wine, whereas a varietal name identifies a grape. An origin may also carry production rules, and the grape need not appear on the label. Reading a named origin requires learning its permitted or characteristic grapes and styles.

citations.locator: Geographical Indication and Grape variety headings

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 EU wine protected-origin terminology: PDO
lessons.assertion: PDO means protected designation of origin. For EU wine, the grapes come exclusively from the specified geographical area and the wine is produced there under its specification. The protected name links the product to its place; it does not by itself certify that a taster will prefer it to every PGI wine.

citations.locator: Protected designation of origin: wine-specific origin and production rules

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 EU wine protected-origin terminology: PGI
lessons.assertion: PGI means protected geographical indication. For EU wine, at least 85% of the grapes come from the specified area and the wine is produced there under its specification, compared with exclusively local grapes for PDO. These wine rules differ from the simpler one-production-stage explanation used for many food products.

citations.locator: Protected geographical indication: the wine-specific 85% rule, distinguished from food products

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 ripeness effects: white aroma and flavour
lessons.assertion: For suitable varieties, less ripe fruit can suggest citrus or green/orchard-fruit character, while riper fruit can suggest stone or tropical fruit and very ripe fruit may appear dried or cooked. These are comparative tendencies: variety, site and winemaking matter, and every white grape does not follow one identical sequence.

citations.locator: Where your wine comes from and Grape variety: broad climate/ripeness flavour tendencies
Fruit ripeness: fresh versus very ripe/cooked character

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 ripeness effects: black aroma and flavour
lessons.assertion: Within a suitable variety, less ripe fruit may retain herbaceous or tart fruit character; riper fruit can show fuller ripe-fruit character, and extra-ripe fruit may suggest dried or cooked fruit. Red-fruit versus black-fruit associations also depend on variety and growing conditions; neither colour descriptor is a universal ripeness measurement.

citations.locator: Where your wine comes from: broad red-fruit/black-fruit/dried-fruit tendencies
Aroma/Flavour and Phenolic Compounds: varietal character and herbaceousness
Fruit ripeness: fresh versus very ripe/cooked character

lessons.dimension: L2 LO1 ripeness effects: tannin maturity
lessons.assertion: Sugar accumulation, flavour development and seed/skin phenolic maturity need not progress at the same rate. As seeds mature and brown, their tannins can become less extractable; skin and seed observations help assess the intended red-wine style. No single Brix value, seed colour or taste proves complete ripeness or guarantees a soft finished wine.

citations.locator: Grape Seeds and Aroma/Flavour and Phenolic Compounds: differing maturity rates and extractability

lessons.dimension: L3 LO1 vine structure: one-year and permanent wood
lessons.assertion: A shoot is current-season green growth. Mature portions become woody canes; a cane retained from the previous growing season is one-year wood carrying buds for the next season. The trunk and retained arms or cordons form older permanent structure. These parts are distinguished by age and function, rather than treated as interchangeable stems.

citations.locator: Grapevine terminology: shoot, cane, arm and cordon

lessons.dimension: L3 LO1 vine structure: green parts
lessons.assertion: Current green shoots carry leaves, buds and tendrils, together with inflorescences that can develop into grape bunches. Leaves supply photosynthate through photosynthesis. Green seasonal growth is distinct from the retained woody framework that supports growth in later years.

citations.locator: Grapevine terminology: shoot with leaves, tendrils and clusters
Budburst, shoot growth, flowering and fruit set

lessons.dimension: L2 LO2 oak vessels: small versus large
lessons.assertion: For similarly shaped vessels with comparable wood, age, toast and contact time, a smaller oak vessel exposes each litre of wine to more wood surface than a larger one, favouring greater extraction of oak compounds. A large old vessel can therefore support maturation with little oak flavour; size alone does not determine the result.

citations.locator: Page 4, The volume effect: wood surface per litre decreases with increasing volume
Oak reuse and variables affecting extractable wood compounds

lessons.dimension: L2 LO2 oak vessels: toast
lessons.assertion: Heating oak during coopering changes the wood compounds available to the wine, altering aromas such as toast or smoke and the character of oak tannins. Heating time and intensity, wood and extraction conditions matter; a heavier toast is not simply more of every oak aroma and is not a quality ranking.

citations.locator: Toast levels: thermal change, aromatic substances and oak-tannin degradation
Toasting and oak composition

lessons.dimension: L2 LO2 blending aim: complexity
lessons.assertion: Blending components with complementary aromas, flavours or textures can create additional sensory layers in the finished wine. Components may come from different varieties, parcels or vessels, including the same variety. The aim differs from balancing acidity or maintaining a house style; adding more components does not automatically improve complexity or quality.

citations.locator: How are wines blended? and Enhance complexity

lessons.dimension: L3 LO1 red fermentation: cap management definitions
lessons.assertion: A pump over removes fermenting liquid from below the floating skin cap and returns it over the cap, wetting the solids and renewing liquid–skin contact. This can aid extraction and redistribute heat; oxygen exposure depends on the setup. Frequency and intensity are selected for the grapes and intended style, rather than maximised automatically.

citations.locator: Cap management: pump-over operation, contact and process variables

lessons.dimension: L3 LO1 red fermentation: cap management comparison
lessons.assertion: A punch down pushes the floating skins down into the fermenting liquid instead of pumping liquid over them. Renewed contact helps extract colour and tannin and manage the cap. The effect depends on timing, force, frequency and fruit; either operation must be adapted to the desired wine rather than assumed intrinsically gentler or better.

citations.locator: Cap management: punch-down operation and variables
